name: Ambassy

origin.parentage: A more highly coloured sport (clone) of Delcorf / Delbarestivale, which is itself Golden Delicious x Stark Jonagrimes

history: A French colour sport of Delcorf (sold in Britain as Delbard Estivale), selected for a redder skin and marketed by the French nursery Dalival under the names Ambassy and Dalili. The National Fruit Collection received it in 1994. Some fruit guides simply treat it as another trade name for Estivale.

look.description: Yellow apple heavily washed and streaked with orange-red, more brightly coloured than ordinary Delcorf.

taste.summary: Sweet, crisp and juicy, with enough acidity to taste fresher than its Golden Delicious parent. Tasters of the Delcorf family pick out light strawberry and pear hints; the cream flesh bruises easily but stays crisp for a couple of weeks.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, within two to three weeks of picking

tree.notes: Grows like Delcorf: a productive spur-bearer that holds its fruit well, but crops need thinning or the apples stay small and the tree may slip into alternate bearing.

pollination.notes: Group taken from the parent clone Delcorf/Estivale (group 3). Needs a diploid partner flowering at the same time. One NFC record shows Ambassy in bloom unusually early, so a group 2-3 partner is a safe choice.

climate.best_climates: Temperate western Europe with warm but not baking summers, such as France, the Low Countries and southern England, where the Delcorf family is grown commercially.
climate.poor_climates: In very hot summers early apples like this soften quickly and the red colour, which is the whole point of the sport, develops poorly; cold short-season areas are also marginal.

health.other: Average susceptibility to scab and mildew reported by the nursery. The fruit bruises easily, so handle gently at picking.

grow_notes: A good early red apple for a sunny site on fertile, well-drained soil. Thin the fruitlets in June to keep size up and help prevent biennial cropping, and plant a group 2-3 diploid nearby for pollination.

name: Bakers Delicious

origin.place: Wales (found); introduced by Bakers nursery, Codsall, near Wolverhampton

history: A Welsh find, brought into commerce in 1932 by the Bakers nursery at Codsall near Wolverhampton. It has nothing to do with the American Delicious; the name refers to the nursery. Specimens are kept in the National Fruit Collection and in the Marcher Apple Network collections.

look.description: Medium, slightly conical yellow apple with a light orange to orange-red flush broken into streaks.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained cream flesh that is crisp and juicy, with a pleasantly aromatic flavour that has more depth than many early apples. Best eaten soon after picking as it does not keep long.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, fresh from the tree

tree.notes: Little published growing data. Treat as an ordinary early dessert apple and prune as a spur-bearer until it shows otherwise.

pollination.notes: Usually listed in an early flowering group (2), consistent with National Fruit Collection blossom dates. Not independently confirmed; assume it needs a pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist western Britain and similar maritime climates, where it was found and is still kept in collections.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or continental climates; like most early English apples it would probably ripen soft and poorly coloured in a hot summer.

grow_notes: A heritage early apple suited to gardens in the west and Midlands. Give it a sunny spot on reasonably drained soil and pick over two or three visits as the fruit colours, eating it straight away.

name: Beauty of Bath
history: Found at Bailbrook near Bath and put on the market by the Bath nursery of George Cooling around 1864; it gained an RHS First Class Certificate in 1887. For decades it was Britain's main commercial early apple, and growers spread straw under the trees to cushion the fruit as it dropped. It is a likely parent of Discovery.

look.description: Flattish, rather small-to-medium apple, pale greenish-yellow flushed and streaked bright red; the white flesh is often stained pink under the skin.

taste.summary: Soft, very juicy flesh with a sharp, refreshing bite that turns sweeter if eaten the moment it ripens. It has a distinctive early-summer tang but goes mealy within a day or two of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Early-mid Aug, straight off the tree; does not keep

tree.notes: Makes a large, broad, flat-topped tree. Ripe fruit falls readily, so pick in several passes as the apples colour, or grass the ground beneath to soften the drop.

pollination.notes: Usually placed in RHS flowering group 2 (one source lists 3). Needs a diploid partner flowering early to mid season.

climate.best_climates: Cool and mild, damp climates such as western and southern Britain, where it ripens in early August with good colour; it was also widely planted in northern and eastern Europe.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers make the already short-lived fruit soften and drop even faster and dull the colour.

health.other: Generally healthy and scab-resistant. Main faults are heavy fruit drop at ripening, very short shelf life, and some bitter pit.

grow_notes: Best on a vigorous-to-medium rootstock in a garden where someone can pick and eat the apples daily during early August. It needs room to spread, and an early-flowering pollinator such as another group 2 or 3 diploid.

name: Benenden Early

origin.parentage: Saint Edmund's Pippin x Lady Sudeley

history: Raised around 1945 in Southampton by J. J. Gibbons and introduced in 1952 by the Stuart Low nursery at Benenden in Kent, which gave it its name. A rare variety today, held in the National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Large, broadly round-conical, sometimes irregular fruit; greenish-yellow skin largely covered with orange-red streaks.

taste.summary: Soft, rather coarse yellowish flesh with a mild, gently acidic flavour. An early apple to eat straight from the tree rather than store.
taste.best_eaten: Mid-late Aug, straight from the tree

tree.notes: Few growing records. Prune as a normal spur-bearing dessert apple.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published. National Fruit Collection blossom dates put it close to Discovery and James Grieve, so a mid-season (group 3) diploid partner is likely to overlap.

climate.best_climates: Southern English conditions, where it was raised and ripens in mid August.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot or very cold regions; its soft early fruit would probably deteriorate fast in hot summers.

grow_notes: A curiosity for collectors of Kent and southern English apples. Plant in full sun on fertile, free-draining soil and pick over a couple of weeks in August, eating the fruit fresh.

name: Bethan

origin.parentage: Thought to be Rajka x Sunrise (raised from seed in 2015)

history: A small early dessert apple from Karim Habibi's seedling programme, named after his wife Bethan and introduced in 2022.

look.description: Small yellow apple with a red flush and pale cream flesh.

taste.summary: A small, crisp, juicy and sweet early apple with more richness than most September fruit; the RHS fruit specialist Joan Morgan called it pretty and moreish.

grow_notes: No independent growing information found. Follow the supplying nursery's advice on rootstock and pollination partners.

name: Delprim
history: Raised in the late 1960s by the Delbard nursery at Malicorne in central France, one of several Delbard early apples descended from Delbarestivale. The National Fruit Collection took it in in 1982.

look.description: A red-skinned early apple; detailed descriptions are scarce.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy flesh with a light, moderately aromatic flavour. Like most very early apples it is for eating within a week or so of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Mid-late Aug, within a week of picking

tree.notes: A fairly vigorous, heavy-cropping spur-bearer; choose a dwarfing rootstock for small gardens.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2); pair with another early or early-mid season diploid.

climate.best_climates: Temperate France and southern England, where Delbard's early apples were selected and trialled.
climate.poor_climates: Little evidence from other climates; early apples generally soften quickly in hot summers, and its early blossom is at risk in frost pockets.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded. Early flowering exposes the blossom to late frosts.

grow_notes: Plant away from frost pockets because it blossoms early. Thin heavy sets so the fruit sizes up, and harvest in mid August for immediate eating.
